messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan, a 32-year-old South Asian man, had been working as a housekeeper for five years when his life took a drastic turn. One evening, while walking home from work, he was mugged by a group of teenagers in an alleyway near his apartment complex. The memory of that night remained etched in his mind like a fresh wound. When the memory returned, as it often did, Rohan felt physical pain in the same parts of his body where he had been kicked and punched during the assault. His memories of the event were vivid and detailed – the smell of garbage, the sound of laughter, and the feeling of helplessness. Rohan's wife, Priya, noticed a change in him after that night. He became increasingly withdrawn and started questioning everyone around him. "People are not what they seem," he would say to her, his eyes clouded with suspicion. Rohan couldn't shake off the feeling that anyone could be a potential threat, just like those teenagers who had attacked him for no reason. His mistrust extended beyond strangers; even friends and family members seemed untrustworthy in his eyes. As time passed, Rohan's memories of the mugging became more intertwined with his growing sense of paranoia. When he recalled the event, he couldn't help but think that it was a stark reminder of how the world is a truly dangerous place. His memories served as evidence to support his negative appraisals – proof that people were inherently untrustworthy and that the world was hostile. Rohan's occupation made things worse. As a housekeeper, he had to interact with new people every day, which only fueled his mistrust. He would often find himself wondering if the guests whose rooms he cleaned might be hiding something or plotting against him. These thoughts would lead him back to memories of that fateful night, and he would feel the same wave of pain wash over him. Priya tried to reassure Rohan, but her words seemed hollow in the face of his lived experience. His memories and negative appraisals had formed a vicious cycle, each reinforcing the other until it became hard for him to distinguish between reality and paranoia. The world outside felt like a battlefield, and Rohan felt constantly on edge, waiting for the next attack. It was when he started noticing changes in his work performance – missed deadlines, forgotten tasks, and strained relationships with colleagues – that Rohan realized he needed help. He couldn't shake off the feeling that he was losing himself to these memories and negative appraisals. With a deep sense of desperation, he reached out for therapy, hoping to break free from this cycle of pain and mistrust. Rohan's current state is one of quiet despair. As he sits in his living room, surrounded by familiar comforts, he can't help but wonder if the world will ever feel safe again. What brings him hope is the possibility that therapy might help him rewire his thoughts, learn to trust others once more, and find a way to silence the echoes of that fateful night.
